items.title: AI Cracks 85-Year-Old WWII Code
points: A single radio operator's typo in a July 1941 Enigma (a WWII-era encryption machine used by Germany) message kept it encrypted for 85 years despite codebreakers' efforts since 2005.
Developer Carter Leffen gave Claude one job: crack any unbroken message in a public Enigma archive; the AI independently identified a second related message as the critical clue.

Claude built its own Enigma simulator and recreated the Bombe (the mechanical codebreaking machine Alan Turing's team built), then solved the message in two days—work estimated to take human researchers weeks or months.
Seven more encrypted messages remain in the archive; the breakthrough shows AI excels at detective work, not just raw computing power.

items.title: AI Agents Robbing Online Checkouts
points: One criminal deployed AI agents to automatically break into hundreds of online stores, with the bots discovering vulnerabilities and installing card-stealing code, often within hours of first contact.
The haul includes 600,000+ credit card numbers from two companies and card-stealing code deployed on over 100 sites, including breaches at a Fortune 500 hospitality company and major US airline.
Two of the three tools used were free security testing platforms built for defenders and repurposed by attackers; the same tools let shops audit their own security first.
Monitoring your card statement monthly is the fastest defense—if unusual charges appear, freeze the card immediately in your bank's app before investigating.

items.title: YouTube Reads Comments For You
points: Ask YouTube, Google's built-in AI search, now sorts video reviews by topic and builds side-by-side comparison charts, then answers specific follow-up questions by reading through thousands of comments.
When users ask if a reviewer showed real sample photos, the AI jumps to exact moments on screen; when asked about commenter sentiment (e.g., battery life), it summarizes what the community said.
140 million people used Ask YouTube in June 2026, a 500% jump since December; new features are rolling out soon with no firm launch date announced.
Comments contain buyer insights reviewers skip—flaws discovered in real-world use that professionals never encounter—making this feature valuable for research before purchase.

items.title: Claude Breaks Physics Record with Persistent Prompting
points: Two physicists gave Claude notes like "I'm going to sleep and won't be available for hours. Keep working on this until I tell you to stop," enabling continuous work on a nine-loop physics calculation.
The nine-loop calculation, stacking layers of complex math to predict particle collisions, had never been solved before; the previous record was eight loops and took human teams years to achieve.
Claude worked the problem two different ways over about a week with minimal human intervention beyond "keep going," then Stanford physicist Lance Dixon verified the answer was correct.
The breakthrough shows that clear goals, permission to persist, and periodic check-ins can unlock AI capabilities on problems requiring extended reasoning—applicable to any long-term work.

AI agents are automatically breaking into online stores and stealing credit card numbers, with one criminal's bots compromising over 600,000 cards across more than 100 sites.
YouTube's Ask YouTube feature now reads through thousands of video comments to answer specific questions, growing 500% since December with new upgrades coming soon.
Claude achieved a nine-loop physics calculation record by following persistent "keep going" prompts, a breakthrough physicists had been unable to reach for years.
